newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen promises quick release of Russian hostages.
newsitem.headline: Chechen promises quick release of Russian hostages.

text.p: A top Chechen official on Sunday said 22 Russian Interior Ministry troops held hostage in Chechnya for the past day would be released on Monday.
Russian officials had earlier warned Chechen separatist leaders that the seizure of the troops could halt Moscow's military withdrawal from the region, news agencies said.
"The Russian policemen will be handed over to the Russian authorities tomorrow," First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov told NTV commercial television.

Hardline Chechen field commander Salman Raduyev acknowledged that his fighters had taken the Russians into custody, and said they would be released later on Sunday, his spokeswoman told reporters in Grozny. Udugov's later comments suggested that the return of the Russians had been delayed.
As many as 60 armed Chechen fighters arriving by car and bus seized the Russians on Saturday near the Dagestan-Chechnya border, said Russian Interior Ministry spokesman Arkady Pashtushkov.

Raduyev led a hostage-taking raid into Dagestan last January, prompting a large-scale Russian military rescue effort during which 26 Russians and about 150 Chechens died. The Chechen military leader escaped badly wounded.
Two years after it launched a full-scale military assault on Chechnya to quash the region's moves towards independence, Russia last month agreed to pull out its remaining troops from the region.

Three top Russian officials in the region overseeing Chechen policy sent Chechnya's president a memorandum warning that unless the Russians were released, Moscow could halt the withdrawal of its forces, Interfax news agency said.

"These provocations could have irreparable consequences that could lead up to stopping the withdrawal of federal forces and the peace process in Chechnya as a whole," the agency quoted the document as saying.
Government officials in Moscow said they could not immediately confirm details of the memorandum.

Chechen leaders, anxious to ensure that Russian troops leave the region before a general election scheduled for January 27, have denounced similar incidents in the past and moved to resolve them quickly.
Raduyev said his soldiers seized the Russians after they were stopped on the road to Dagestan, where they were invited to attend a conference, his spokeswoman said.

After the Russian interior ministry troops radioed back to their headquarters and were told to detain the Chechens, the Chechen forces disarmed the Russians and took them into custody as a pre-emptive move, Raduyev's spokeswoman said.
The commander of Russia's Interior Ministry troops said the Chechens used women and children to help disarm the Russians, RIA news agency said.
The Chechens "sent the women, old people, and children ahead of them, who mingled with the militiamen and thus prevented them from opening fire," it quoted Anatoly Shkirko as saying.

Russia sent soldiers into Chechnya in December 1994 to crush a three-year independence bid, but the military failed to win control of the region and are now pulling out after being humiliated by determined Chechen fighters.
Tens of thousands of people, most of them civilians, were killed in 21 months of fighting.
